title: PowerShell vs. WSL
subtitle: Which shell should drive your AI agent's daily automation on Windows?

powershell.detail: PowerShell ships with every modern Windows install. There is nothing to set up before an agent can start running commands.

wsl.detail: A single admin command installs WSL2 plus a default Ubuntu distribution. Requires one restart, then it behaves like a permanent Linux machine.
wsl.example:
wsl --install
# restart Windows when prompted
# launch it any time with: wsl

powershell.detail: Most agent skills, install scripts, and copy-pasted tutorial commands assume a POSIX shell. An agent has to translate bash idioms into PowerShell on the fly, and translations don't always land cleanly.

wsl.detail: Commands an agent generates from training data or from a README almost always assume bash. In WSL those commands can be pasted in and run exactly as written.

powershell.detail: Windows-native package managers exist, but their command syntax and package names rarely match what a tutorial written for Mac/Linux shows.
powershell.example:
winget install Python.Python.3.12
winget install Git.Git

wsl.detail: The exact package managers most tutorials reference — installs behave identically to a Mac or a Linux server.
wsl.example:
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y python3-pip
pip install mkdocs mkdocs-material

powershell.detail: Windows-style paths use backslashes and ignore case, which matches every other Windows tool — but breaks scripts written with forward-slash paths.

wsl.detail: POSIX-style paths, exactly like on Mac or Linux. Case matters, so 'Projects' and 'projects' are different directories.

powershell.detail: Direct access to the registry, COM objects, Active Directory, IIS, and Office automation. If the task is genuinely about managing Windows itself, PowerShell is the only real option.

wsl.detail: WSL cannot directly touch the Windows registry, COM objects, or Windows services. It's a Linux environment first — great for cross-platform dev work, not for Windows administration.

powershell.detail: PowerShell reads and writes the Windows filesystem directly, with no translation layer to slow it down.

wsl.detail: Working on files under the Windows drive from inside WSL (/mnt/c/...) crosses a filesystem boundary and is noticeably slower. Keep project repos inside WSL's own filesystem (~/) instead.
wsl.example:
# Slow: crosses the WSL/Windows boundary
cd /mnt/c/Users/Dan/projects

# Fast: lives natively inside WSL
cd ~/projects

powershell.detail: Quoting rules, aliases that only look like their bash namesakes (ls, cat), and object-based pipes cause AI-generated commands to fail or behave unexpectedly more often.
powershell.example:
# Looks like bash, behaves differently:
ls -la
# PowerShell's 'ls' is an alias for Get-ChildItem
# and doesn't support the -la flag combo at all

wsl.detail: Commands generated by an AI agent, copied from a tutorial, or pulled from a skill's script almost always run correctly on the first try, since they were written with bash in mind.

powershell.detail: The mkdocs command itself runs fine once the environment is active, but getting there can involve execution-policy prompts and PATH troubleshooting that look nothing like the Mac/Linux instructions most guides give.
powershell.example:
conda activate mkdocs
mkdocs gh-deploy
# common snag: Set-ExecutionPolicy
# needed before scripts are allowed to run

wsl.detail: Identical to publishing from a Mac. No execution-policy prompts, no PATH archaeology — just activate the environment and deploy.

source: See the "PowerShell vs. WSL" appendix for the full write-up and reasoning behind this comparison.
